newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rate cut seen unlikely in next 12 months.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rate cut seen unlikely in next 12 months.

text.p: Prospects of a cut in interest rates later this year are fast receding and South Africans will likely have to wait another 12 months for relief, acording to the largest investment group, Old Mutual.
Chief economist Dave Mohr said on Wednesday cyclical reasons for an rate cut appeared convincing but several factors supported continued high rates.

"The case for a cut in rate looks fairly watertight but events happening on the ground, such as further exchange control relaxation in July, suggest caution," Mohr told reporters at the group's latest economic monitor presentation.

Factors working against an early interest rate cut included high money supply growth, additional measures to relax exchange controls, which required high interest rates to discourage an exodus of local capital, and the recent increase in U.S. rates.
"Money supply and credit growth are still way above the Reserve Bank's target growth and we still need hard evidence that inflation is falling," Mohr said.
"Those expecting a rate cut this year could once more be dissapointed."
Despite clear signals in the economy that spending growth was tailing off and would continue to do so for most of the year, an outright recession was unlikely in the current economic cycle, he added.
Positive signs were that the production side of the economy was showing growth.

Non-agricultural production rose an annualised 2.5 percent in the fourth quarter last year while the revival of the manufacturing sector -- which makes up a quarter of total GDP -- conmtinued into the first quarter of 1997.
One of the factors behind growth in the manufacturing sector was the weaker rand which put domestic manufacturers in a better position to compete.
But Mohr said the recovery in the rand this year could unwind some of the positive features supporting manufacturing.
"There are worries that the rand is too strong to support the underlying features in the economy," he said.
After firming around 20 cents since the beginning of the year, the rand has traded at between 4.40 and 4.50 against the dollar since early February.

Despite the revival in the manufacturing sector, the financial side of the economy had been disappointing with the foreign trade surplus slumping in the first two months of the year, worryingly low foreign exchange reserves and stubbornly high money supply and credit demand growth.
Mohr issued a "health warning" to consumers over record debt levels.
He said the old "buy now, pay later with cheap money" psychology still existed but credit based spending could prove very costly if inflation remained tame and real interest rates high.
Private sector demand for credit ballooned to almost 380 billion rand in February -- the latest statistics available -- up 17.34 percent from a year ago and 1.8 percent month-on-month.
